  - paragraph:
    - text: "Songshan Airport was not part of the first Neihu alignment: the project record says the Ministry of Transportation ordered a feasibility study in ROC 89 (2000) for a station that would directly serve airport trips."
    - superscript:
      - link "[1]":
        - /url: "#ref-1"
    - text: DORTS reports that the evaluation found an airport station on the Neihu Line more feasible in engineering terms and compatible with the construction schedule, after which the route was adjusted and the station added.
    - superscript:
      - link "[1]":
        - /url: "#ref-1"
    - text: The same project record says the Executive Yuan agreed in principle in ROC 90 (2001), the Public Construction Commission agreed to the funding arrangement in ROC 91 (2002), and the revised project cost was NT$60.997 billion.
    - superscript:
      - link "[1]":
        - /url: "#ref-1"
    - text: The route leaves its elevated approach at Minzu East Road, enters the airport, and places the station beneath the surface car park in front of the terminal building.
    - superscript:
      - link "[1]":
        - /url: "#ref-1"
    - text: The project table identifies the airport station as BR1 in the Neihu engineering sequence, while the operating station is BR13 ; the two identifiers belong to different numbering systems.
    - superscript:
      - link "[1]":
        - /url: "#ref-1"
    - text: The CB420 section starts east of the station, uses shield tunnels below Songshan Airport, crosses the expressway and Keelung River, reaches Dazhi, and continues to the point where the line emerges for its elevated section.
    - superscript:
      - link "[5]":
        - /url: "#ref-5"
    - text: That section is about 3,460 metres long, with separate airport tunnel drives of 1,241 metres and 1,286 metres for the down and up lines.
    - superscript:
      - link "[5]":
        - /url: "#ref-5"
    - text: The two drives passed below the runway, apron and taxiway, and the published cover decreases from 27.8 metres near the Huajiang Street ventilation shaft to 18.8 metres at the airport-station end.
    - superscript:
      - link "[5]":
        - /url: "#ref-5"
    - text: DORTS records the airport crossing as Taipei Basin K1 lake-deposit ground, with a 50-to-60-metre layer of very soft silty clay whose low self-support and sensitivity made settlement a central construction concern.
    - superscript:
      - link "[5]":
        - /url: "#ref-5"
    - text: Because airport rules constrained when workers could enter and observe the site, the monitoring system combined automatic reading and transmission with manual observation during the night-time airport closure.
    - superscript:
      - link "[5]":
        - /url: "#ref-5"
    - text: The down-line shield drive launched on 8 October 2003 and reached the station diaphragm wall on 30 June 2004; the up-line drive launched on 8 September 2004 and arrived on 7 September 2005.
    - superscript:
      - link "[5]":
        - /url: "#ref-5"
    - text: DORTS’s architecture account calls the station’s design concept “A Story of Flight”, using spiral-wing steel roofs to link the entrances and accessible lift and to suggest a pair of wings waiting to depart.
    - superscript:
      - link "[2]":
        - /url: "#ref-2"
    - text: That account also describes a ground plaza, water feature and curved ventilation-shaft wall as a combined place for activity, rest and artistic work rather than treating the entrance as only a circulation object.
    - superscript:
      - link "[2]":
        - /url: "#ref-2"
    - text: The official art table records Great Age of Travel at Exit 3, Flight Plan on the concourse wall and Dream Flight in the platform void, completed in October 2008 through open selection.
    - superscript:
      - link "[3]":
        - /url: "#ref-3"
    - text: DORTS’s broader public-art record says Neihu works other than the donated Gangqian piece were funded through the Neihu Line construction budget, with DORTS handling selection and valuation and its eastern works office handling contracts, material subsidies and implementation.
    - superscript:
      - link "[4]":
        - /url: "#ref-4"
    - text: The checked CB420 and project pages identify the section and programme but do not publish an individual station contractor, award date or final station-package value, so those fields remain TBC.
    - superscript:
      - link "[5]":
        - /url: "#ref-5"

  - paragraph:
    - text: Zhongxiao Fuxing is the central interchange between the Wenhu and Bannan lines.
    - superscript:
      - link "[12]":
        - /url: "#ref-12"
    - text: The project record brings the original Muzha corridor through Fuxing South and North Roads before it reaches Zhongshan Junior High.
    - superscript:
      - link "[1]":
        - /url: "#ref-1"
    - text: The high-elevated-station volume places it in CC403 with Songshan Airport, Zhongshan Junior High and Nanjing East Road, and gives the station a 70-metre platform.
    - superscript:
      - link "[2]":
        - /url: "#ref-2"
    - text: DORTS’s station-planning manual identifies Zhongxiao Fuxing as a non-parallel interchange where vertical circulation joins platforms at different levels.
    - superscript:
      - link "[12]":
        - /url: "#ref-12"
    - text: TRTC’s current page places the Wenhu and Bannan transfer corridor near Exit 2 and records separate paid-area facilities for the two lines.
    - superscript:
      - link "[13]":
        - /url: "#ref-13"
    - text: The joint-development site covers the southwest side of the Zhongxiao East Road Section 3 and Fuxing South Road intersection, with a total development area of 7,691 square metres.
    - superscript:
      - link "[10]":
        - /url: "#ref-10"
    - text: DORTS’s concept design joined the building’s first through third floors to the Wenhu facilities and its basement levels one through three to the Bannan entrances.
    - superscript:
      - link "[10]":
        - /url: "#ref-10"
    - text: The city published the development plan in November 1997, sought investors in March 1999, signed the investment contract in January 2000 and recorded completion and an occupancy permit in November 2006.
    - superscript:
      - link "[10]":
        - /url: "#ref-10"
    - text: The project was planned for retail and department-store use, with public paid parking and reserved connections to the rapid-transit facilities.
    - superscript:
      - link "[10]":
        - /url: "#ref-10"
    - text: DORTS later described the Zhongxiao Fuxing building as one of the larger city-managed development assets and recorded a unified-management model with investor Hongtong.
    - superscript:
      - link "[11]":

    - text: The same management record says the original proposal had six basement levels and thirteen floors above ground, but the transit mezzanine was counted as an additional floor, producing a six-basement, fourteen-floor design.
    - superscript:
      - link "[11]":
        - /url: "#ref-11"
    - text: The common Muzha station design used curved roofs, aluminium panels, laminated glass, platform doors and transparent lifts, with no platform air-conditioning.
    - superscript:
      - link "[6]":
        - /url: "#ref-6"
    - text: DORTS later judged that the heavy outer frames reduced the intended lightweight transparency of the standardised station image.
    - superscript:
      - link "[5]":
        - /url: "#ref-5"
    - text: The live TRTC log records a 2 August 2026 signalling anomaly in the Zhongxiao Fuxing section that briefly stopped trains for about two minutes while the rest of the line remained unaffected.
    - superscript:
      - link "[14]":
        - /url: "#ref-14"
    - text: The same log records a 5 August passenger medical emergency at the station; the system continued normal operation while station staff used an AED assessment and CPR before handing over to paramedics.
    - superscript:
      - link "[14]":
        - /url: "#ref-14"
    - text: The Muzha section opened on 28 March 1996 as Taiwan’s first driverless medium-capacity metro.
    - superscript:
      - link "[9]":
        - /url: "#ref-9"
    - text: The individual CC403 contractor, award date and final station-package value are not identified in the full primary pages checked here, so those fields remain TBC.

    - text: At programme level, DORTS places the first-phase works within 21 civil, water, environmental and electromechanical section contracts, alongside separate systems packages for rolling stock, signalling, power, communications, depot equipment, automatic-fare collection and track; this is a delivery structure, not a station price.

    - superscript:
      - link "[6]":
        - /url: "#ref-6"
    - text: DORTS’s construction table calls this station Y06, while the current operating records call it Y07 ; the builder’s engineering identifier is retained here as historical contract context rather than silently converted into the operating code.
    - superscript:
      - link "[6]":
        - /url: "#ref-6"
    - text: The DF111 design brief links the Dapinglin section to the Liugong Canal, Shisizhang farmland and the Xindian River crossing, treating those water, agricultural and river landscapes as the local design context.
    - superscript: "[?]"
    - text: For that section, DORTS describes the “nature” theme through square geometry in façades and seating and through the use of the line colour in interior elements, so the design vocabulary connects the civil corridor to the passenger-facing architecture.
    - superscript: "[?]"
    - text: The official line-wide art record identifies the public-art procurement as commissioned creation and reports a design fee of NT$16,000,000; that amount belongs to the corridor-wide commission, not to this station alone.
    - superscript:
      - link "[7]":
        - /url: "#ref-7"
    - text: That record describes the commission as extending across roughly 212 elevated columns, about 8 kilometres of beams, about 10 kilometres of sound barriers, platform doors at all 14 stations, selected façades and vertical walls, and train exteriors and interiors.
    - superscript:
      - link "[7]":
        - /url: "#ref-7"
    - text: The checked DORTS records therefore establish the station’s construction-package setting, landscape brief and share of a line-wide art programme, but they do not publish a Y07 -only civil final account or a separate station art budget.

  - paragraph:
    - text: DORTS records the Ankeng civil turnkey award on 3 March 2016, the main works start on 6 April 2016, and a line-wide budget of NT$16.632 billion.
    - superscript:
      - link "[4]":
        - /url: "#ref-4"
    - text: The route project record describes the depot at the Antai and Anyi roads, then the first five passenger stations following Anyi Road before the alignment turns onto elevated Anhe Road at K06 .
    - superscript:
      - link "[4]":
        - /url: "#ref-4"
    - text: A separate builder engineering record places the three-bore Shuang’an Tunnel and its light-rail track crossover in the section between K01 and Ankeng Depot.
    - superscript:
      - link "[6]":
        - /url: "#ref-6"
    - text: That tunnel record distinguishes the depot lead from a tunnel between passenger stations, making the underground work part of the operating approach rather than a buried K01 – K02 segment.
    - superscript:
      - link "[6]":
        - /url: "#ref-6"
    - text: In February 2021, DORTS reported track laying at K01 and K02 on what its progress article calls the at-grade section, with depot track work scheduled next.
    - superscript:
      - link "[10]":
        - /url: "#ref-10"
    - text: The same progress record describes the 2.6-hectare depot as a deliberately small facility divided into stabling, maintenance and administration areas.
    - superscript:
      - link "[10]":
        - /url: "#ref-10"
    - text: By the end of 2021, the depot and K01 – K05 systems had been energised so trains could begin on-line testing, according to the builder’s January 2022 progress report.
    - superscript:
      - link "[12]":
        - /url: "#ref-12"
    - text: An earlier October 2021 milestone recorded the first train entering the depot, completed at-grade civil and track work, and continuing elevated track and electromechanical work.
    - superscript:
      - link "[14]":
        - /url: "#ref-14"
    - text: That milestone set out static, dynamic and endurance tests as the next sequence, connecting the physical completion of the K01 approach with the later systems-validation programme.
    - superscript:
      - link "[14]":
        - /url: "#ref-14"
    - text: The power-system design takes 161 kV from Taipower supply points into the K05 and K09 utility rooms, steps it down to 22.8 kV, and distributes it to the line’s traction substations.
    - superscript:
      - link "[13]":
        - /url: "#ref-13"
    - text: Those substations rectify the traction supply to 750 V direct current for the trains, although the technical article does not assign a separate traction substation to K01 itself.
    - superscript:
      - link "[13]":
        - /url: "#ref-13"
    - text: The builder later identified China Steel as electromechanical turnkey contractor, China Engineering Consultants as project manager, and Sinotech Engineering Consultants as supervision consultant.
    - superscript:
      - link "[16]":
        - /url: "#ref-16"
    - text: The electromechanical project received New Taipei’s Public Construction Golden Quality Award in December 2023, with the award article also noting a 42 percent vehicle-domestication ratio.
    - superscript:
      - link "[16]":
        - /url: "#ref-16"
    - text: DORTS presents the route as a connection for the Anyi and Anhe communities and estimates that the project can shorten relevant trips by roughly 15 to 20 minutes.
    - superscript:
      - link "[4]":
        - /url: "#ref-4"

            - text: Converted VAL256 units return to passenger service, running alongside the Innovia fleet
            - superscript:
              - link "[1]":
                - /url: "#ref-1"
    - paragraph:
      - text: So for nearly eighteen months the whole 24-station line ran on the Bombardier fleet alone, while the trains that had opened the railway sat in a depot having their control system replaced. Why the line was re-signalled at all — and why by a competitor of the system's owner — is told on
      - link "The Matra dispute":
        - /url: /rail/history/matra-dispute/
      - text: .
    - paragraph:
      - text: The original equipment was a fixed-block ATC/ATO system derived from the MAGGALY technology on Lyon Metro line D
      - superscript:
        - link "[2]":
          - /url: "#ref-2"
      - text: ; what replaced it is a moving-block communications-based system.
    - heading "Design" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - text: VAL vehicles run on rubber tyres over concrete running surfaces, and are guided from the
      - strong: sides
      - text: ", not the centre: pairs of horizontal wheels bear outward against lateral guide bars — H-section steel, set roughly 200 mm above the running surface on either side of the vehicle — and those same bars carry the 750 V supply, which is why a VAL guideway needs no separate conductor rail"
      - superscript:
        - link "[3]":
          - /url: "#ref-3"
      - superscript:
        - link "[4]":
          - /url: "#ref-4"
      - text: .
    - paragraph:
      - text: VAL's own successor went the other way. The NeoVal generation Siemens announced in 2006
      - emphasis: is
      - text: centrally guided, on a single rail similar to Translohr's
      - superscript:
        - link "[4]":
          - /url: "#ref-4"
      - text: . Central guidance is VAL's future, not its past, and Taipei has the past.
    - heading "The formation is not fixed" [level=3]
    - paragraph:
      - text: Cars are delivered and counted in pairs — DORTS bought 51 of them under contract CC350
      - superscript:
        - link "[8]":
          - /url: "#ref-8"
      - text: — and two pairs make a four-car train. But
      - strong: the pairs are not permanently married into sets
      - text: ": zh.wikipedia describes this fleet as 「非固定編組」, a non-fixed formation, with a train made up of four consecutively-numbered cars rather than of one unchanging four-car unit"
      - superscript:
        - link "[9]":
          - /url: "#ref-9"
      - text: .
    - paragraph:
      - text: That detail does more work than it looks.
      - link "TRTC":
        - /url: /rail/operators/trtc/
      - text: "'s own announcement of the seat-removal programme counts"
      - strong: 25 four-car trains
      - superscript:
        - link "[10]":
          - /url: "#ref-10"
      - text: ", and 25 trains is 50 pairs against a fleet of 51. If the sets were fixed, that odd pair would be a permanent orphan needing an explanation. If the formation is not fixed, there is nothing to explain — the cars run as 25 trains"
      - superscript:
        - link "[10]":
          - /url: "#ref-10"
      - text: and which cars those are is a maintenance question rather than a fact about the fleet
      - superscript:
        - link "[9]":
          - /url: "#ref-9"
      - text: .
    - paragraph:
      - strong: Confidence is Medium and the page does not overstate it.
      - text: The pair counts and the train count are both primary; 非固定編組 is one encyclopedia, and no manufacturer or operator document found says it. It is also the reading that resolves the
      - link "line-level arithmetic problem":
        - /url: /rail/metro/lines/wenhu-line/
      - text: without requiring a train formed from both fleets, which is a reason to want it to be true and therefore a reason to mark it carefully.
    - heading "Fleet history" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - text: Ordered for the Muzha Line and in service from its opening on 28 March 1996, originally working BR01 through BR12 only. Since December 2010 the fleet has run the full route alongside the
      - link "Innovia APM 256 (C370)":
        - /url: /rail/metro/rolling-stock/innovia-apm-256-c370/
      - text: .
    - paragraph:
      - emphasis: Delivery dates by unit, and the scope of the re-signalling work on each set, are still to be confirmed.
    - heading "Depot allocation" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - text: Maintained at
      - link "Muzha Depot":
        - /url: /rail/metro/depots/muzha-depot/
      - text: ", beside BR01 , which also stables Innovia sets"
      - superscript:
        - link "[7]":
          - /url: "#ref-7"
      - text: .
    - heading "Corrections" [level=2]
    - list:
      - listitem:
        - strong: This page previously said the fleet was re-signalled ahead of the 2009 extension.
        - text: "That inverts the sequence: the conversion began the day the extension opened and the fleet was out of service until December 2010"
        - superscript:
          - link "[1]":
            - /url: "#ref-1"
        - text: .
      - listitem:
        - strong: This page previously said VAL vehicles are guided by horizontal wheels bearing on a central rail.
        - text: They are side-guided
        - superscript:
          - link "[3]":
            - /url: "#ref-3"
        - superscript:
          - link "[4]":
            - /url: "#ref-4"
        - text: . The likely origin of the error is the NeoVal succession — the
        - emphasis: later
        - text: generation is centrally guided, and the two were run together here.

- main:
  - navigation "Breadcrumb":
    - link "Home":
      - /url: /
    - link "Rail & cable":
      - /url: /rail/
    - text: The network
  - link "Back to the Stations index":
    - /url: /rail/metro/stations/
  - heading "The network" [level=1]
  - paragraph: 10 lines, 192 stations. 9 of the lines are drawn below from Taiwan MOTC route geometry; the Sanying Line is newer than MOTC’s extract, so its 12 stations are outside that station count and it is drawn dashed, as a chain of the operator’s published station points rather than as surveyed track. Colours are the official ones each operator publishes — not the values circulating in English-language sources, which are all slightly wrong.
  - paragraph:
    - strong: The Sanying Line is drawn as a chain of station points, not as an alignment.
    - text: "It opened on 30 June 2026. The New Taipei Metro line records this map is built from carry a source update stamp of 23 May 2023 — nearly three years earlier — and return one line, the Circular Line. There is no LB route geometry to draw. What its dashed line joins is its twelve stations, in the operator’s published order, at the New Taipei City landmark register’s own coordinates: it states where the stations are and what sequence they run in, and states nothing about the route between them. The line is written up from the operator’s own announcement on its"
    - link "line page":
      - /url: /rail/metro/lines/sanying-line/
    - text: . It
    - emphasis: is
    - text: in the table below, in its own colour, taken from the operator’s LB line mark.
  - figure:
    - img
    - text: "Every line the site carries, each labelled with its code at both ends — colour alone does not identify a line. Bannan blue and Airport MRT purple are indistinguishable to a reader with protanopia, and Tamsui red against Danhai red is the closest pair on the network even in normal colour vision, which is why every line carries its code. Interchange stations are ringed in black; termini are the outer dots. Branch track is drawn as a pale core of its parent's colour inside a hairline of the same colour darkened — a branch belongs to its line rather than being a line of its own, and the hairline is what gives the pale core a defined edge on the paper. 4 lines have one: Tamsui-Xinyi, Songshan-Xindian, Zhonghe-Xinlu and Danhai LRT. Where a line appears broken, the alignment across the gap is missing from the published geometry — those breaks are holes in the source data, not features of the network, and are left unbridged rather than joined with track we cannot evidence. A dashed line is not surveyed track: it joins that line's published station points in order and says nothing about the route between them. Sanying is drawn that way, having no published route geometry at all."

  - paragraph:
    - strong: Length is official; Measured is ours.
    - text: "The operators publish a route length through TDX — as a running total against the last station of each route, not in the route-length field, which is zero throughout. Measured is computed independently from the surveyed geometry, taken between the outermost stations because the published alignment runs on past both termini into depot leads and tail track. The two agree to within about 150 m on every line whose geometry is continuous, which is the point of printing both: the check is visible rather than asserted. Both columns describe the trunk route only, so a line's branch is excluded from each. A ≥ marks a line whose geometry arrives in discontinuous runs — the track crossing each gap is absent from the source, so our figure is a floor, and the shortfall against the official column measures how much is missing: 0.8 km on the Tamsui–Xinyi Line, 2.8 km on the Circular. End-to-end times are MOTC's own."
  - paragraph:
    - strong: A † marks a figure that is not the platform's.
    - text: MOTC's data holds no record of the Sanying Line of any kind — not a line record, not a station, not a metre of geometry — so its station count, length and end-to-end time on this table are the operator's own, from New Taipei Metro's own opening announcement, 30 June 2026, and are cited on its
    - link "line page":
      - /url: /rail/metro/lines/sanying-line/
    - text: . The length bar is drawn to the same scale as every other, because a published route length is the same quantity whoever published it; what the dagger marks is that this row was assembled from a different source than the 9 above it, not that it is worth less. Its colour is the operator's too — see
    - link "the line colours page":
      - /url: /data/line-colours/
    - text: for where that was read and what it was checked against.

  - paragraph: "The 捷運 network as this site files it: TRTC's lines, New Taipei Metro's Circular, Sanying and light rail lines, and Taoyuan Metro's Airport MRT. Three companies, and from a rider's point of view one railway — one stored-value card, one interchange network, one station-numbering scheme, one map."
  - paragraph: "That is the boundary this system draws, and it is the boundary the fare system draws. It is not drawn by technology: the network contains rubber-tyred metro, steel-wheel metro and street-running light rail, and none of those is a reason to file a line somewhere a rider would not look for it. Taiwan Railway and high speed rail are outside it because they are separate networks with separate ticketing, separate stations and separate operators — not because they are a different kind of train."

- main:
  - figure "Maokong Station, the gondola's upper terminus. CEphoto, Uwe Aranas · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons":

  - heading "Cable" [level=1]
  - paragraph: The Maokong Gondola — an aerial ropeway run by a TRTC subsidiary, and the region's only cable transit.
  - heading "Lines All lines →" [level=2]:
    - text: Lines
    - link "All lines →":
      - /url: /rail/cable/lines/
  - paragraph: The gondola itself — route, stations, cabins and the T16 incident history.
  - list:
    - listitem:
      - link "Maokong Gondola Taipei's first cable car and Taiwan's longest — a TRTC-family ropeway whose T16 tower was undermined by a 2008 typhoon, investigated by the Control Yuan, and rebuilt 30 metres from where it stood.":
        - /url: /rail/cable/lines/maokong-gondola/
  - heading "Stations All stations →" [level=2]:
    - text: Stations
    - link "All stations →":
      - /url: /rail/cable/stations/
  - paragraph: The Maokong Gondola's four passenger stations, each researched from the operator's own per-station pages rather than restated from the line article.
  - list:
    - listitem:
      - link "Maokong Station The line's upper terminus and namesake — a three-storey rotating-platform building at the centre of the hillside tea-house district, 299 metres up from where the ride began.":
        - /url: /rail/cable/stations/maokong-station/
    - listitem:
      - link "Zhinan Temple Station A T-shaped elevated station at Zhinan Temple's own rear-mountain car park — one of the two stations directly affected by the 2008–2010 T16 tower closure, since both lie on the closed side of the line.":
        - /url: /rail/cable/stations/zhinan-temple-station/
    - listitem:
      - link "Zoo South Station The only one of the gondola's four stations to carry a different name today than the one it opened with — renamed from Zoo Interior Station eight years after opening, which is why the Control Yuan's own 2009 report on this line still calls it by the old name.":
        - /url: /rail/cable/stations/zoo-south-station/
    - listitem:
      - link "Zoo Station The gondola's lower terminus — a separate structure roughly 350 metres from the Wenhu Line's own Taipei Zoo station, not a shared platform, joined only by an out-of-station transfer.":
        - /url: /rail/cable/stations/zoo-station/
  - paragraph: "One system, one line: the Maokong Gondola. It is an aerial ropeway — a POMA installation, not a railway — and it is filed here rather than under its own top-level heading because a heading for a single line is a heading that says nothing. What it shares with the rest of this section is the thing this section is organised by: it runs on its own fixed guideway, to published stations, in a published order, inside the region's stored-value ticketing, and it meets the metro at Taipei Zoo."
  - paragraph: "The gondola is part of the network in the ways that matter here: metro affiliation, shared ticketing, and a genuine engineering and incident history that English coverage — which is entirely tourist-oriented — has not touched. The story worth telling is the long typhoon closure: a tower foundation undermined, a multi-institute engineering assessment, and a reopening under monitoring. That is the kind of material this site exists for, and it will be written against the city's own engineering publications rather than travel blogs."
  - paragraph

      - text: Maokong Station is the gondola's upper terminus, at 指南路三段38巷35號, an elevation of
      - strong: 299.3 metres
      - superscript:
        - link "[2]":
          - /url: "#ref-2"
      - text: — roughly 275 metres higher than
      - link "Zoo Station":

      - superscript:

      - superscript:

      - text: .       - superscript:
        - link "[1]":
          - /url: "#ref-1"
      - text: . Local bus connections named on the operator's page include the right-hand loop of the Maokong sightseeing bus and routes 小10 and 棕15

ticketing-fare-stages.snapshot:
- main:
  - navigation "Breadcrumb":
    - link "Home":
      - /url: /
    - link "Ticketing":
      - /url: /ticketing/
    - link "Guides":
      - /url: /ticketing/guides/
    - text: How bus fare stages (段) actually work
  - link "Back to Guides":
    - /url: /ticketing/guides/
  - article:
    - heading "How bus fare stages (段) actually work" [level=1]
    - paragraph: Taipei and New Taipei buses do not charge one flat fare. They charge by the number of fare "segments" (段) a trip crosses, and where those segment points fall is not published as one complete list anywhere — only two examples are ever officially named.
    - region "Quick facts":
      - text: How bus fare stages (段) actually work
      - term: Legal basis
      - definition:
        - text: 臺北市公共汽車客運業營運管理自治條例, Article 11
        - superscript:
          - link "[2]":
            - /url: "#ref-2"
      - term: Full fare
      - definition:
        - text: NT$15 per segment
        - superscript:
          - link "[3]":
            - /url: "#ref-3"
      - term: Student fare (EasyCard)
      - definition:
        - text: NT$12 per segment
        - superscript:
          - link "[3]":
            - /url: "#ref-3"
      - term: Concessionary fare
      - definition:
        - text: NT$8 per segment
        - superscript:
          - link "[3]":
            - /url: "#ref-3"
      - term: On-board ticket sales
      - definition:
        - text: None — cash or e-ticket only, no change given
        - superscript:
          - link "[3]":
            - /url: "#ref-3"
    - paragraph:
      - text: Taipei and New Taipei's joint-operation buses do not charge a flat fare. They charge by
      - strong: 段 (段次)
      - text: — fare segments — and a rider who does not know where the segment points fall on their own route has no reliable way to predict whether a trip costs one fare or two before boarding.
    - heading "The rule, and its legal basis" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - text: "Under 臺北市公共汽車客運業營運管理自治條例 (the Taipei City ordinance governing bus operations), Article 11 sets the underlying principle: a bus operator's fare should be uniform in principle, but a route with a longer run may instead be charged by segment or by distance"
      - superscript:
        - link "[2]":
          - /url: "#ref-2"
      - text: . Article 9 of the same ordinance requires that the fare segment point (or buffer zone) be posted on the physical stop sign itself, alongside the terminus name, first/last bus times and headway
      - superscript:
        - link "[2]":
          - /url: "#ref-2"
      - text: — the segment structure is not meant to be a surprise at tap-out, at least not by design.
    - paragraph:
      - text: "Taipei's Public Transport Office states the practical version of the rule plainly: 「本市聯營公車依據「臺北市公共汽車客運業營運管理自治條例」第11條規 定採分段收費制，同時參採橋樑、河流等自然分界及重要轉運點（如華中橋、臺北車 站等）訂定，並無長度及站數之強制要求，跨越分段點即加收1段票」"
      - superscript:
        - link "[1]":
          - /url: "#ref-1"
      - text: ". In English: segment points are sited using natural boundaries — bridges, rivers — and major transfer hubs, with"
      - strong: no fixed rule for how long a segment has to be or how many stops it must cover
      - text: . Crossing a segment point (or its buffer zone) simply adds one segment's fare.
    - paragraph:
      - text: "New Taipei's own city buses run on the identical mechanic. The joint Taipei/New Taipei bus portal states it for both cities in one sentence: 「雙北市區公車係依路段分段收費，搭乘2段票(含)以上路線之車輛，若跨越分段點 (或分段緩衝區)，應加收1段票」"
      - superscript:
        - link "[3]":
          - /url: "#ref-3"
      - text: .
    - heading "What a segment actually costs" [level=2]
    - table:
      - rowgroup:
        - row "Fare class Cash EasyCard/e-ticket":
          - columnheader "Fare class"
          - columnheader "Cash"
          - columnheader "EasyCard/e-ticket":
            - link "EasyCard":
              - /url: /ticketing/guides/cards-passes-and-fares/
            - text: /e-ticket
      - rowgroup:
        - row "Full fare NT$15 NT$15[3]":
          - cell "Full fare"
          - cell "NT$15"
          - cell "NT$15[3]":
            - text: NT$15
            - superscript:
              - link "[3]":
                - /url: "#ref-3"
        - row "Student NT$15 NT$12 (an 8-fold/20%-off card rate)[3]":
          - cell "Student"
          - cell "NT$15"
          - cell "NT$12 (an 8-fold/20%-off card rate)[3]":
            - text: NT$12 (an 8-fold/20%-off card rate)
            - superscript:
              - link "[3]":
                - /url: "#ref-3"
        - row "Concessionary (elderly, disabled/companion, eligible children) NT$8 NT$8[3]":
          - cell "Concessionary (elderly, disabled/companion, eligible children)"
          - cell "NT$8"
          - cell "NT$8[3]":
            - text: NT$8
            - superscript:
              - link "[3]":
                - /url: "#ref-3"
    - paragraph:
      - text: "That per-segment rate is confirmed twice, independently: once by the joint government fare portal, and once by the operators' own trade association, which publishes the identical NT$15/12/8 structure on its own site"
      - superscript:
        - link "[4]":
          - /url: "#ref-4"
      - text: . Buses do not sell tickets on board and do not give change — the fare portal is explicit that payment is cash
      - emphasis: or
      - text: stored-value card, with no other option, and no change is made for cash overpayment
      - superscript:
        - link "[3]":
          - /url: "#ref-3"
      - text: . Children under 115cm ride free outright; children 115cm or taller but under 6 with an identity document also ride free; one fare-paying adult may bring up to four such children at no charge
      - superscript:
        - link "[3]":
          - /url: "#ref-3"
      - text: .
    - heading "Where the segment points actually are" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - text: "Officially, not many are named at all. Taipei's Public Transport Office's own FAQ gives exactly two worked examples: 華中橋 (Huazhong Bridge) and 臺北車站 (Taipei Main Station)"
      - superscript:
        - link "[1]":
          - /url: "#ref-1"
      - text: . No government source fetched for this page publishes a complete list of every segment point on the network — Article 9 requires each one to be posted at its own stop, but that is necessarily a stop-by-stop disclosure, not a single published index.
    - paragraph:
      - text: Chinese Wikipedia's own article on Taipei's city buses offers a longer, nine-location list of what it calls "common" segment points —
      - link "Shilin":
        - /url: /rail/metro/stations/r16/
      - text: (士林),
      - link "Dazhi":
        - /url: /rail/metro/stations/br14/
      - text: (大直),
      - link "Taipei Bridge":
        - /url: /rail/metro/stations/o13/
      - text: (臺北橋), Taipei Main Station, the Zhonghua Road north/south stops, Wanhua (萬華), the wholesale produce market (果菜市場),
      - link "Gongguan":
        - /url: /rail/metro/stations/g07/
      - text: (公館), and
      - link "Songshan":
        - /url: /rail/metro/stations/g19/
      - text: (松山) — mostly major transfer hubs or bridgeheads at the old Taipei City/County boundary
      - superscript:
        - link "[6]":
          - /url: "#ref-6"
      - text: . That list is not attached to any citation on the Wikipedia page itself, and it notably does
      - strong: not
      - text: include Huazhong Bridge, which is one of only two locations the regulator names directly
      - superscript:
        - link "[1]":
          - /url: "#ref-1"
      - text: . Both lists are published here as what they are — one official but minimal, one fuller but unverified — rather than merged into a single confident list.
    - heading "How crossing multiple segments is counted" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - text: "Chinese Wikipedia's article on New Taipei's own city buses gives a worked example of the counting logic. For a corridor running through zones A, B and C, with B as the segment point: riding within one zone, or from A to B, or from B to C, is one segment; riding all the way from A to C is two segments (the single-segment fare, doubled)"
      - superscript:
        - link "[7]":
          - /url: "#ref-7"
      - text: . On a longer corridor with two segment points, A–B–C–D–E, both B and D count as crossing points
      - superscript:
        - link "[7]":
          - /url: "#ref-7"
      - text: . This is an illustrative example rather than a government fare rule in itself, but it does not contradict, and directly illustrates, the primary rule already confirmed above.
    - heading "How many segments does a route actually have?" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - text: "There is no fixed one-to-four-segment ceiling. Counting directly over this project's own already-committed New Taipei route-service data — 562 routes with a published fare row — segment counts run from 1 to 8: 128 routes are 1-segment, 77 are 2-segment, 37 are 3-segment, 13 are 4-segment, 8 are 5-segment, 3 are 6-segment, and 3 reach 8 segments, alongside a handful of free routes"
      - superscript:
        - link "[5]":
          - /url: "#ref-5"
      - text: . Taipei-proper's own committed bus dataset does not carry a comparable segment-count field, so that same distribution for Taipei's own colour- and series-numbered routes is not established here.
    - heading "How this interacts with transfers and the regional pass" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - text: The bidirectional MRT–bus transfer discount — NT$8 for an ordinary card, NT$6 for a student card, NT$4 for a welfare card, within a 60-minute window — applies against a segment fare the same way it applies against any bus fare
      - superscript:
        - link "[8]":
          - /url: "#ref-8"
      - text: . That same FAQ's own title is explicit that the discount excludes "distance-charged buses" (里程收費公車) — a separate, named fare category outside the segmented system this page describes, and one this project has not yet independently researched
      - superscript:
        - link "[8]":
          - /url: "#ref-8"
      - text: .
    - paragraph:
      - text: "The TPASS 基北北桃1200都會通 regional pass sidesteps the segment system entirely for a pass holder: its own operating notice confirms unlimited rides at unlimited distance on both Taipei's joint-operation network and New Taipei's city buses"
      - superscript:
        - link "[9]":
          - /url: "#ref-9"
      - text: . A pass holder does not pay per segment at all — there is no separate multi-segment surcharge or cap to interact with.
    - heading "What this page does not yet say" [level=2]
    - list:
      - listitem:
        - strong: A complete, official list of Taipei's segment points.
        - text: Only two are confirmed directly from a primary source; a longer secondary list exists on Wikipedia but is unverified and self-describes as only the "common" ones, not an exhaustive account.
      - listitem:
        - strong: Taipei-proper's own segment-count distribution
        - text: ", as opposed to New Taipei's, which is established above from already-committed project data."
      - listitem:
        - strong: What specifically defines a "distance-charged" (里程收費) bus route
        - text: ", how many exist, and how their fares are structured — named as an exception category in an existing FAQ title, but not itself researched for this page."
    - region "Specifications":
      - heading "Specifications" [level=2]
      - table:
        - rowgroup:
          - row "Officially named segment-point examples Huazhong Bridge, Taipei Main Station [1]":
            - rowheader "Officially named segment-point examples"
            - cell "Huazhong Bridge, Taipei Main Station"
            - cell "[1]":
              - superscript:
                - link "[1]":
                  - /url: "#ref-1"
          - row "New Taipei published routes, segment range (committed data) 1–8 [5]":
            - rowheader "New Taipei published routes, segment range (committed data)"
            - cell "1–8"
            - cell "[5]":
              - superscript:
                - link "[5]":
                  - /url: "#ref-5"
          - row "MRT–bus transfer discount, ordinary card 8 NT$[8]":
            - rowheader "MRT–bus transfer discount, ordinary card"

              - text: NT$
              - superscript:

  - paragraph: Every English-language source we could find has Taipei's metro line colours wrong. Not badly wrong — most are within a few percent — but not one of the seven matches what the operators actually publish. These are the official values, taken from Taiwan's Ministry of Transportation and Communications, with the working shown.
  - 'link "Official line colours All 10 lines: hex values, swatches, contrast against white and black, and where each one was read. Plus a reconciliation against the Wikipedia and Wikidata values — including one case where a citation to an official route map was further from correct than the value it replaced, and one line the platform does not carry at all. 10 lines · 9 from MOTC TDX"':

  - link "Station records All 192 stations across 10 lines — codes, Chinese and English names, coordinates where published, interchanges and running order. TDX-backed records are downloadable as JSON; Sanying's twelve records cite the operator on their station pages. 192 stations · mixed provenance":
    - /url: /data/stations/
  - link "Bibliography Every source cited anywhere on this site, marked primary or secondary, with the pages that rest on it and the date each URL was read. The primary-to-secondary ratio is the honest summary of how much of this site is first-hand. Cited sources · primary vs secondary":
    - /url: /data/sources/

  - paragraph: All of this is derived from Taiwan government open data and is reproduced here under the same terms. If you are building something and need Taipei Metro line colours or station records, take them — a link back is welcome but not required.

  - heading "The one that is not from TDX" [level=2]
  - paragraph:
    - text: The Sanying Line opened on 30 June 2026 and has no record on the platform of any kind — no line record, so no
    - code: LineColor
    - text: to read. Every operator code on TDX was probed for it; New Taipei's two light rail lines turned out to be filed under codes of their own, and there is no equivalent for Sanying.
  - paragraph:
    - text: "What settled it was the operator's own line mark: New Taipei Metro publishes the LB roundel on its Sanying Line station page as a 156×156 lossless PNG, and the whole ring — a third of the image, to the pixel — is"
    - code: "#48B6D2"
    - text: . That is the operator rendering its own line identity at a known value on its own site, which is the same kind of thing a
    - code: LineColor
    - text: field is, read out of a different file.
  - paragraph:
    - strong: The PANTONE figure is a genuine loose end.
    - text: "“PANTONE 637C” circulates for this line and could not be confirmed anywhere: not on the operator's site, not on the New Taipei rapid transit bureau's route page or its identity page, and not in either Wikipedia article — all of which say only 淺藍色, light blue. Nor is it a value you could simply adopt: the third-party PANTONE-to-sRGB converters disagree among themselves ("
    - code: "#4EC3E0"
    - text: ","
    - code: "#4DC5E2"
    - text: ","
    - code: "#42BFDF"
    - text: ","
    - code: "#48A8D0"
    - text: ), so taking the designation on trust would still mean picking one conversion over three others. The table above records the commonest of them against the operator's own value; the difference is what it is, and this page is not going to resolve it by choosing.
  - heading "A warning about citation chains" [level=2]
  - paragraph: Two of these are worth dwelling on, because they show a failure mode that is easy to repeat.
  - paragraph:
    - text: This site originally carried
    - code: "#B57A28"
    - text: for the Wenhu Line. That was replaced with
    - code: "#C48C31"
    - text: on the strength of a Wikidata value
    - emphasis: citing TRTC's own route map
    - text: — which sounds authoritative and is the kind of provenance you would normally accept. The official value is
    - code: "#B57A25"
    - text: . The correction moved the value further from the truth than the guess it replaced.
  - paragraph:
    - text: The same thing happened with the Airport MRT. An earlier
    - code: "#8246AF"
    - text: was replaced by
    - code: "#8E47AD"
    - text: from Wikidata. The official value is
    - code: "#8246AF"
    - text: — exactly what was discarded.
  - paragraph:
    - text: The lesson is not that Wikidata is unreliable. It is that
    - strong: a citation to an official source is not the same as the official source
    - text: ", and confidence in a chain of references is not evidence about what sits at the end of it. Where a government publishes the data through an API, use the API."
  - heading "Caveats" [level=2]
  - list:
    - listitem:
      - strong: Circular and Airport MRT are not TRTC.
      - text: Circular is New Taipei Metro and the Airport MRT is Taoyuan Metro, so their colours come from those operators' records. A request limited to TRTC returns five lines.
    - listitem:
      - strong: These are screen values.
      - text: DORTS states its signage system defines Pantone, RGB and CMYK values per line; that specification is not published openly and may not match these hex values exactly. The Sanying Line is the case where that gap is visible rather than theoretical — see above.
    - listitem:
      - strong: The source data is not new.
      - text: See

  - heading "Provenance" [level=1]
  - paragraph: Which facts on this site are official records, which are our own research, and which are still open. A reference site that will not tell you this is asking you to take it on trust.
  - paragraph:
    - strong: The source data is not current.
    - text: We retrieved it on 2026-08-10, but the operators' own last-updated stamps run from
    - strong: 2020-01-31
    - text: to 2026-08-05. That is fine for a network which has not changed since — but a station opening after those dates will not appear here, and no amount of refetching changes that until the operator republishes.
  - heading "Who publishes what" [level=2]
  - paragraph: Taipei's network is run by three companies, and they do not publish identical datasets. If you are building on this data, this is the table you want before you start.

    - strong: Zero is not the same as absent.
    - text: Taoyuan Metro publishes a transfer dataset and it is empty — the Airport MRT has no in-system interchanges to record. An em dash means the operator does not publish that dataset at all.
  - heading "Ours — researched, not official" [level=2]
  - list:
    - listitem:
      - strong: Elevated or underground.
      - text: TDX does not publish structure. Ours is compiled by hand and kept in a separate overlay file so refetching official data can never overwrite it — and so it is never mistaken for official data. Two Wenhu stations are marked
      - emphasis: not established
      - text: rather than guessed.
    - listitem:
      - strong: Everything about rolling stock and depots.
      - text: Fleet sizes, car dimensions, capacities, depot areas and stabling capacity are not in any open dataset we have found. Anything marked TBC on those pages is genuinely unknown to us, not merely unfetched.
    - listitem:
      - strong: Measured route lengths.
      - text: Distances computed along the drawn geometry, between the first station and the last. These are ours, and they sit beside the operators' own figures on
      - link "the network page":
        - /url: /rail/network/
      - text: rather than replacing them — printing both is what makes the check visible.
  - heading "Corrected" [level=2]
  - paragraph:
    - text: This site previously said TDX did not publish route length, because the
    - code: RouteLength
    - text: "field on the route record is zero for every metro route. That was wrong, and the data was already in this repository:"
    - code: StationOfRoute
    - text: carries a cumulative distance against every station, and the last one is the route's length. The Wenhu Line is 25.17 km, which settles a figure this site had been recording as unsourced. The lesson is the same one the line colours taught — check the whole record before concluding a source is silent.
  - heading "Still open" [level=2]
  - list:
    - listitem: Which two Wenhu stations are underground.
    - listitem: Where the 25.7 km Wenhu route length in circulation comes from. The official figure is 25.17 km and our own measurement agrees at 25.04 km; 25.7 is unaccounted for.
    - listitem: Headways, track gauge and electrification.
    - listitem: Station opening dates — not published in any dataset we fetch.
    - listitem:
      - text: Whether DORTS's published Pantone and CMYK signage values match the hex values on
      - link "the colours page":
        - /url: /data/line-colours/
      - text: .
  - heading "Licence and reuse" [level=2]
  - paragraph:
    - text: The underlying records are Taiwan government open data, published by MOTC through TDX under the
    - link "Open Government Data Licence":
      - /url: https://data.gov.tw/licenses
    - text: . You may use, reproduce, distribute and adapt them, including commercially, provided you attribute the source.
  - paragraph: Our derived work — the contrast-checked badge and accent colours, the chained geometry, the structure overlay — is offered on the same terms. Attribution to Taipei Transit Guide is welcome but not required; attribution to MOTC is required by their licence, not ours.
  - paragraph: 180 TDX stations · 12 primary-sourced Sanying stations · 5 operators · retrieved 2026-08-10 · sources last updated 2020-01-31 to 2026-08-05

about.snapshot:
- main:
  - navigation "Breadcrumb":
    - link "Home":
      - /url: /
    - text: About
  - link "Back to the previous page":
    - /url: /data/provenance/
  - heading "About" [level=1]
  - paragraph: An English-language reference for public transport in Taipei, written because the material exists in Mandarin and nowhere else in a form you can look something up in.
  - heading "What this is" [level=2]
  - paragraph: Taipei's transport network is unusually well documented — in Mandarin. Between 批踢踢 (PTT), Mobile01 and the Chinese Wikipedia there is detailed, argued-over coverage of rolling stock, depot allocations, signalling contracts and construction history. Some of it is better than anything published officially.
  - paragraph: "In English there is an encyclopedia article per line and a great deal of visitor-facing advice about which exit to use. What is missing is the layer in between: structured reference material you can look a fact up in, with the source attached. That gap is what this site is for."
  - paragraph: It is independent and non-commercial. It is not affiliated with Taipei Rapid Transit Corporation, New Taipei Metro, Taoyuan Metro, the Taipei City Government or any bus operator, and it carries no advertising.
  - heading "How it sources material" [level=2]
  - heading "Official data where it exists" [level=3]
  - paragraph:
    - text: For the 180 stations the platform carries, names, codes, running order, coordinates, interchanges, route lengths and end-to-end times come from
    - link "TDX":
      - /url: https://tdx.transportdata.tw/
    - text: ", the Ministry of Transportation and Communications' open data platform. So do 9 of the 10 line colours, from the publishing operator's own line record. The exception is the Sanying Line, which opened in June 2026 and has no record on the platform at all; its colour was read instead from the operator's own line mark, and"
    - link "the line colours page":
      - /url: /data/line-colours/
    - text: says exactly which file and what it was checked against. TDX has no Sanying station dataset either, so LB01–LB12 are maintained in a separate hand-researched registry from the operator's station table and twelve information sheets. Every displayed Sanying fact links to that primary evidence, and coordinates remain TBC. The generated TDX registry itself is not hand-edited.
  - paragraph:
    - text: That decision has already paid for itself twice. Every English-language line colour we could find was wrong, including two cases where a confident correction citing an official map moved
    - emphasis: away
    - text: from the official value — the working is on
    - link "the colours page":
      - /url: /data/line-colours/
    - text: . And the route length this site published was 1.4 km too long, because it measured geometry that runs past both termini into depot leads, while the operator's own figure sat unread in a field nobody had looked in.
  - heading "Mandarin sources, synthesised rather than translated" [level=3]
  - paragraph: Where official data stops — fleet histories, depot facilities, the Matra contract dispute, why a line was built the way it was — the material is in Mandarin. The policy is to read it, cross-check it, and write it in English from scratch, citing the original in its own language rather than an English mirror of it. Translating a forum thread wholesale would be both a copyright problem and a way of importing its errors without noticing them.
  - paragraph: Where sources disagree, the intention is to record every value rather than pick the most plausible one and present it as settled.
  - heading "TBC rather than a guess" [level=3]
  - paragraph:
    - text: A figure marked
    - emphasis: TBC
    - text: means nobody here has traced it to a source worth citing. It does not mean the number is unknown to the world. It would be easy to fill those gaps with figures that are probably right, and the site would look more finished; it would also stop being usable as a reference, because you could no longer tell which numbers had been checked.
  - paragraph:
    - text: The same applies structurally. The
    - link "bus section":
      - /url: /bus/
    - text: is empty and says so rather than being hidden. Where a figure has been settled since — the two underground Wenhu stations were marked “not established” for four builds and are now named, from the builder’s own record and an encyclopedia agreeing from different directions — the page says how it was settled rather than quietly filling the gap.
  - heading "Citations, and a count of what has none" [level=3]
  - paragraph:
    - text: Every page carries a source list, and a figure that rests on one says so with a numbered mark you can follow. Each entry records the title in English and in the original language, the publisher, the date the URL was read, and whether the source is
    - strong: primary
    - text: — the operator, the builder, a government department, a court — or
    - strong: secondary
    - text: ". That last field is required and has no default: this site has already found a case where a citation to an official route map was further from the published colour than the value it replaced, so who says a thing has to travel with the thing."
  - paragraph:
    - text: Everything cited anywhere is collected in the
    - link "bibliography":
      - /url: /data/sources/
    - text: ", with the primary-to-secondary ratio stated at the top. It is currently about a third primary, which is not good enough and is published anyway."
  - paragraph:
    - text: The build also counts statements that carry
    - emphasis: "no"
    - text: source at all, separately from those marked TBC, and refuses to let that number grow. A labelled gap and an unlabelled assertion are different failures, and only one of them is honest.
  - heading "What is not used" [level=3]
  - paragraph: No operator's route map, photography or signage artwork. Those are copyrighted. The maps on this site are drawn from published coordinate geometry, and the line colours are the published hex values — a colour specification is a fact, an operator's specific map is a design.
  - paragraph:
    - link "Data provenance":
      - /url: /data/provenance/
    - text: sets out field by field what is official, what is researched here, what is derived, and what is still open.
  - heading "Where it has got to" [level=2]
  - paragraph: This is version 1. Every line now has a page written from primary sources, and the Wenhu Line — the first one built, and the one this site went deepest on — also has a page per station, built from official records. 4 of the 103 written pages still carry a stub flag, meaning some figures on them still need tracing to a primary source.
  - paragraph:
    - text: All 192 stations across the network are registered, so any station code on the site validates and any of them can be looked up on
    - link "the station records page":
      - /url: /data/stations/
    - text: ", and every one of them now has a page of its own — position, district, coordinates, interchanges, and run times where its source publishes them. Wenhu's 24 go further: TDX does not publish structure, street exits or engineering numbers, so those come from a hand-built overlay, plus a photograph for every station. A station on another line is a plain TDX read until someone researches it the way Wenhu was researched. Sanying's 12 are the other exception: primary-sourced station records, with unavailable fields shown as TBC rather than inferred from maps."
  - heading "Corrections" [level=2]
  - paragraph: "Corrections are welcome, and specific ones are most useful: the page, the figure, and what it should be, with a source. A source in Mandarin is as good as one in English, and often better."
  - paragraph: The most valuable corrections are the ones that catch something stated confidently and wrongly, rather than something already marked TBC — a gap that is labelled is doing its job, but a wrong figure presented as checked undermines everything next to it.
  - paragraph:
    - strong: Reporting a correction.
    - text: Open an issue on the repository this site is built from, quoting the page URL and the figure in question. If you would rather not use an issue tracker, the same information sent any other way is just as welcome — what matters is the source, not the channel.
  - heading "How it is built" [level=2]
  - paragraph: Content is Markdown; the site is generated as static HTML and served as files, with no server and no runtime API calls. Station code badges, Chinese language tagging, strip maps and geographic maps are all produced at build time from the data, which is why a station code that is not real fails the build rather than rendering as though it were.
  - paragraph: Station and line data retrieved from MOTC TDX on 2026-08-10. Government open data, used under the Open Government Data Licence.
